title: Easements: what can be an easement
subtitle: The Ellenborough Park checklist — four characteristics, and how far they stretch
objectives: State and apply the four characteristics of an easement identified in Re Ellenborough Park
Explain why Hill v Tupper failed the accommodation requirement and how Moncrieff and Regency Villas have since stretched what the doctrine can accommodate
Apply the ouster principle to distinguish a valid easement from a grant that deprives the servient owner of all reasonable use of their own land

leadingAuthorities.role: Sets out the four characteristics an easement must have; confirms a right to use a communal garden can itself be an easement
A right must accommodate the dominant tenement, not merely confer a personal or commercial advantage on the person who happens to hold it
Relaxes the ouster principle — a right can be an easement even if it leaves the servient owner very limited practical use of the land, provided some reasonable use remains possible in law

leadingAuthorities.citation: Regency Villas Title Ltd v Diamond Resorts (Europe) Ltd [2018] UKSC 57
leadingAuthorities.role: Confirms a right to use recreational and sporting facilities can accommodate the dominant tenement and satisfy Ellenborough Park, extending the doctrine well beyond simple access or utility rights

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Almost every easements problem question is secretly the same question asked four times: does this right have a dominant and servient tenement, does it accommodate the dominant land, are the two owners different people, and is the right capable of forming the subject matter of a grant? Learn the checklist once and every fact pattern becomes an audit, not a puzzle.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You can recite the four characteristics. What trips people up is running all four against a fact pattern instead of stopping at the first one that looks satisfied — the test pool below is built to catch exactly that habit.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 2 and make sure you can name all four Ellenborough Park characteristics cold before moving on — the later cases only make sense as extensions of a checklist you already know.

overview.hook: A timeshare owner in Wales has never met the neighbouring landowner, has no contract with them, and yet has a legal right to use their swimming pool, golf course and squash courts — a right that survives even if the timeshare changes hands. It sounds like a licence. The Supreme Court says it can be an easement. This lesson is the four-part test that decides which.

parts.heading: Why 'easement' needs a checklist at all
parts.voice: checklist — frames the whole lesson as a four-part audit run against any right
body: An easement is a right one landowner has over a neighbour's land — a right of way, a right to run a drain across it, a right to light through a window. What makes easements tricky isn't defining the concept in the abstract; it's that the label gets claimed for all sorts of arrangements that don't actually qualify, from a personal permission to park to a commercial deal that happens to involve land.

Re Ellenborough Park is the case every subsequent easements problem is built on. It didn't just decide whether the residents of a Regency square in Weston-super-Mare could use the communal garden at its centre — it produced a four-part test for what can be an easement at all, still applied unchanged today.

Treat what follows as a checklist to run in full, every time, rather than a definition to recognise on sight. A right can look exactly like an easement and fail on a single characteristic — and the exam question is usually hiding the failure in the one you'd be tempted to skip.

components.definition: The dominant tenement is the land that benefits from an easement; the servient tenement is the land burdened by it. An easement cannot exist 'in the air' — it must attach to and benefit a specific piece of land, not merely a person.

interaction.prompt: Can a right exist as an easement if it benefits a named individual personally, with no dominant land identified at all?
options: No — an easement must attach to and benefit a dominant tenement, not simply a person
Yes — easements can benefit either land or a person, interchangeably
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. A right benefiting a person rather than land might be a licence or a personal contractual right, but it cannot be an easement — the whole structure depends on a dominant tenement that the right runs with.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — this is the first checklist item and it's non-negotiable. An easement is a property right attached to land; without an identifiable dominant tenement, whatever the right is, it isn't an easement.

parts.heading: The four Ellenborough Park characteristics
parts.voice: structural — a reference part students return to before every problem question
body: Run every candidate easement against these four characteristics in order. Fail any one of them, and the right is not an easement — whatever else it might be (a licence, a contractual right, a restrictive covenant).

The fourth characteristic — 'capable of forming the subject matter of a grant' — is the one doing the most hidden work. It bundles together several sub-rules: the right must be reasonably certain in what it permits, it must not require the servient owner to spend money, it must not amount to exclusive possession of the servient land, and it must fall within a recognised category of easement or be a legitimate extension of one.

components.label: The four Ellenborough Park characteristics
points: 1. There must be a dominant and a servient tenement
2. The right must accommodate (benefit) the dominant tenement, not just its current owner personally
3. The dominant and servient owners must be different persons

4. The right must be capable of forming the subject matter of a grant — certain enough, not requiring the servient owner's expenditure, not amounting to exclusive possession, and within (or a fair extension of) a recognised category

components.factsShort: Houses built around a communal garden in Weston-super-Mare were sold with a right for each purchaser to use the garden. The question was whether that right could be an easement attached to each house.
components.ratioShort: A right to use a neighbouring garden for pleasure and recreation, shared with other dominant owners, is capable of being an easement, provided the four characteristics are satisfied.

expanded.facts: When the houses around Ellenborough Park were originally sold, each conveyance granted the purchaser and their successors a right to use the ornamental garden in the centre of the square, in common with other residents. Decades later, the question arose whether this right bound successive owners as an easement, or was merely a personal arrangement that had lapsed.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held the right satisfied all the requirements of an easement: there was a dominant tenement (each house) and a servient tenement (the garden); the right accommodated the houses by making them more attractive and useful as residences, not merely providing a personal perk to whoever happened to live there; the garden was owned separately from the houses; and a right to use a garden for pleasure and recreation was capable of forming the subject matter of a grant, being sufficiently certain and analogous to established categories.
expanded.significance: This is the foundational modern statement of what an easement requires. Every later case in this lesson — Hill v Tupper, Moncrieff, Regency Villas — is either applying, testing, or stretching one of these four characteristics.

interaction.prompt: A student is checking whether a claimed right is an easement. Put these checklist questions in the standard Ellenborough Park order.
items: Is there an identifiable dominant and servient tenement?
Does the right accommodate the dominant tenement, not just benefit its owner personally?
Are the dominant and servient owners different people?
Is the right capable of forming the subject matter of a grant?
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the standard order, and it's worth keeping to — each later question assumes the ones before it are already satisfied.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The order matters less than covering all four, but the conventional sequence starts with the tenements, then accommodation, then separate ownership, then the 'capable of grant' characteristics. Re-run the checklist in that order and it gets easier to spot which one a fact pattern is testing.

parts.heading: Accommodation versus personal advantage: Hill v Tupper
parts.voice: case-narrative — contrasts a failure with the standard it fails against
body: Hill v Tupper is the classic failure case, and it fails on characteristic 2: accommodation. Tupper was granted the exclusive right to put pleasure boats on a canal, by the canal company that owned it. When a rival boat operator, Hill, started competing on the same stretch of water, Tupper sued him — arguing the exclusive right was an easement he could enforce against third parties, not just against the canal company that granted it.

The court rejected this. Tupper's right didn't accommodate any piece of land he owned — he held a nearby inn, but the boat-hire right had nothing to do with using or enjoying that inn as land. It was a purely commercial advantage: a monopoly on a trade, attached to Tupper personally, that happened to be exercised on the canal company's water. Take Tupper out of the inn business entirely and the right would mean exactly the same thing to him — which is precisely the sign that it isn't benefiting land at all.

Compare a right of way benefiting a landlocked field: it doesn't matter who owns the field, the right makes that piece of land more usable however it's used or by whomever. That's accommodation. A right that only makes sense as a commercial monopoly for whoever currently holds it is not.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often say Hill v Tupper failed because the right was 'too commercial' to be an easement, as if easements can never have economic value.
components.whyItsWrong: Plenty of valid easements have obvious economic value — a right of way to a shop, a right to run cables to a business. The problem in Hill v Tupper wasn't that the right had commercial value; it was that the right didn't accommodate any land Tupper owned at all. It was a personal trading monopoly, not a benefit to a dominant tenement.

interaction.prompt: Which right more clearly accommodates a dominant tenement, in the Ellenborough Park sense?
interaction.scenarioA: A right granted to the owner of a landlocked cottage to cross a neighbour's driveway to reach the road, binding whoever owns the cottage from time to time.
interaction.scenarioB: A right granted to a named individual to be the sole operator of an ice-cream van on a neighbour's field, regardless of whether that individual owns any land nearby.
interaction.explanation: A accommodates the cottage — it makes that specific land usable, whoever owns it, exactly like the right of way that would have succeeded on Tupper's facts if he'd claimed one for his inn. B is Hill v Tupper again: a personal commercial monopoly with no connection to any dominant land the claimant owns.

parts.heading: The ouster principle, relaxed: Moncrieff
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the old rule before showing how the House of Lords loosened it
body: Here's the old worry behind characteristic 4: if a right leaves the servient owner with no meaningful use of their own land, is it really an easement, or has it become something closer to ownership — exclusive possession dressed up as a lesser right? This is the 'ouster principle': a right that effectively excludes the servient owner from their own land cannot be an easement.

Moncrieff v Jamieson tested this directly. The claimants had a right to park cars on a small area of the servient owner's land, in circumstances where — given the size of the space — parking there left almost no room for the servient owner to do anything else with it. The House of Lords held it could still be an easement. The question is not whether the servient owner is left with much practical use, but whether they retain any reasonable use in law — including the right to grant the same or similar rights to others, and residual ownership itself.

Lord Scott reframed the test: ask whether the servient owner retains possession and control of the land, even if its practical utility to them is minimal, rather than asking whether they're left with much to actually do with it. That reframing is what lets a near-total parking monopoly still count as an easement rather than a disguised transfer of ownership.

components.title: The ouster principle before and after Moncrieff
components.description: How the test for excessive exclusivity in an easement claim shifted.

nodes.label: Old approach: does the right leave the servient owner with substantial practical use of the land?
Problem: near-exclusive rights (e.g. dense parking) risked failing as 'too exclusive' to be easements
Moncrieff: does the servient owner retain possession and control in law, even with minimal practical use?
Result: a right can be an easement even where it leaves very little practical use, so long as ownership and legal control remain with the servient owner

components.textAlternative: Before Moncrieff, courts asked whether the servient owner retained substantial practical use of the land — a test that put near-exclusive rights like dense parking at risk of failing. Moncrieff reframed the question: what matters is whether the servient owner retains possession and control in law, even if practical use is minimal. The result is that a right can be an easement even where it leaves the servient owner very little to actually do with the land.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that, after Moncrieff, a right can be an easement even if it leaves the servient owner almost no practical use of the land?
sliderLabels: Definitely can still be an easement
interaction.explanation: Moncrieff relaxed the ouster principle: the test is possession and control in law, not how much practical use is left in fact. A near-total exclusion from practical use — as with the parking rights in Moncrieff itself — does not automatically defeat an easement claim.

parts.heading: Regency Villas: how far can accommodation stretch?
parts.voice: checklist-meets-case — returns to characteristic 2 and shows its modern limit
body: Regency Villas Title Ltd v Diamond Resorts (Europe) Ltd took accommodation somewhere Ellenborough Park's communal garden had only gestured towards. Timeshare owners at a Welsh resort had been granted rights, decades earlier, to use recreational facilities on neighbouring land — a golf course, swimming pool, squash courts, and gardens run as part of a separate leisure complex. When the facilities' operator changed and stopped honouring the arrangement, the timeshare owners claimed an easement.

The Supreme Court agreed. It rejected the argument that a right to use active recreational and sporting facilities was too far removed from 'accommodating' land to qualify — the kind of argument that would have succeeded if accommodation meant only passive amenities like a garden to sit in. Recreational use that makes the dominant land significantly more attractive and valuable to occupy, the court held, accommodates that land just as much as a right of way or a right to light does — even where the benefit is 'lifestyle' rather than utilitarian.

Put Ellenborough Park and Regency Villas together and the trajectory is clear: accommodation was never limited to necessities. A garden was already recreational; Regency Villas confirms that a full leisure complex — so long as the right is properly tied to specific dominant land, not just to whoever currently owns a timeshare unit as a matter of contract — can accommodate that land too. The limiting principle isn't 'how recreational is too recreational' — it's whether the right genuinely benefits the land itself, the same question Hill v Tupper asks in reverse.

components.definition: A right accommodates the dominant tenement where it enhances the normal enjoyment of that land, judged objectively — a test now understood, after Regency Villas, to extend to recreational and leisure facilities and not merely to utilitarian rights like access, light, or drainage.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below adapted from Regency Villas, highlight the sentence that states the ratio on accommodation.
interaction.passage: The claimants held rights to use golf, swimming and other recreational facilities on the defendant's land, granted for the benefit of the timeshare apartments. The defendant argued that recreational rights of this kind were too far removed from the utilitarian character of a traditional easement to accommodate the dominant land. The court rejected that submission: a right which significantly enhances the normal enjoyment of the dominant land is capable of accommodating it, whether the benefit conferred is utilitarian or recreational in character. The appeal was allowed and the easement upheld.
interaction.ratioSentence: A right which significantly enhances the normal enjoyment of the dominant land is capable of accommodating it, whether the benefit conferred is utilitarian or recreational in character.

testPool.prompt: List the four characteristics of an easement identified in Re Ellenborough Park.
acceptableAnswers: dominant and servient tenement, accommodation, different owners, capable of forming the subject matter of a grant
testPool.modelAnswer: (1) There must be a dominant and servient tenement; (2) the right must accommodate the dominant tenement; (3) the dominant and servient owners must be different persons; (4) the right must be capable of forming the subject matter of a grant.

testPool.prompt: Which case is the source of the modern four-part test for what can be an easement?
options: Re Ellenborough Park
Hill v Tupper

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four Ellenborough Park characteristics?
options: A dominant and servient tenement must exist
The right must accommodate the dominant tenement
The right must have been registered at the Land Registry within six months of grant
The right must be capable of forming the subject matter of a grant
testPool.trapExplanation: Registration is a separate question about how an easement is protected or made binding on a purchaser — it plays no part in whether a right is capable of being an easement in the first place. Ellenborough Park's four characteristics say nothing about registration.

testPool.prompt: In Hill v Tupper, which characteristic did the claimed right fail on?
options: Accommodation of the dominant tenement
The requirement for a servient tenement to exist at all

testPool.prompt: Put these developments in the accommodation requirement in chronological order.
items: Re Ellenborough Park: a right to use a communal garden for recreation held capable of being an easement
Hill v Tupper: an exclusive commercial boat-hire right held not to accommodate any dominant land
Moncrieff v Jamieson: the ouster principle relaxed to a test of legal possession and control, not practical use
Regency Villas: rights to use recreational and sporting facilities held capable of accommodating dominant land

testPool.prompt: What did Moncrieff v Jamieson change about the ouster principle?
options: It shifted the test from whether the servient owner retains substantial practical use, to whether they retain possession and control in law
It abolished the ouster principle entirely, so no right can ever fail for being too exclusive
It held that only rights of way can ever be exclusive enough to raise ouster concerns
testPool.trapExplanation: Moncrieff relaxed the principle, it did not abolish it — a right that genuinely transfers possession and control (not merely leaves little practical use) can still fail. The correct answer is the reframing of the test, not its elimination.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below adapted from Hill v Tupper, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
testPool.passage: The claimant held an exclusive right, granted by the canal company, to put pleasure boats on the canal for hire. He sought to enforce that right against a rival trader as though it bound third parties generally. A right cannot be an easement where it confers a mere commercial monopoly on its holder without accommodating any land which that holder occupies as owner or tenant. The claim accordingly failed.
testPool.ratioSentence: A right cannot be an easement where it confers a mere commercial monopoly on its holder without accommodating any land which that holder occupies as owner or tenant.

testPool.prompt: A landowner grants their neighbour, who owns an adjoining field with no road access, the right to cross their land to reach the highway. Does this right accommodate the dominant tenement?
options: Yes — it makes the landlocked field usable as land, benefiting whoever owns it from time to time
No — access rights are always treated as personal, not proprietary
No — the right only accommodates the current owner personally, not the field itself
testPool.explanation: This is exactly the kind of right Hill v Tupper contrasts with — it benefits the land itself (making it accessible) rather than being tied to a particular person's trade or identity.

testPool.prompt: A right of way is granted over a driveway so narrow that, when a car is parked exercising the right, the servient owner cannot simultaneously use that strip of land for anything else. Applying Moncrieff, is this fatal to the right being an easement?
options: Not necessarily — the test after Moncrieff is whether the servient owner retains possession and legal control of the land, not whether much practical use remains in fact
Yes — any right that leaves no simultaneous practical use for the servient owner automatically fails the ouster principle
Yes — Moncrieff only applies to parking rights specifically, not to rights of way
testPool.explanation: Moncrieff's reframing is general, not limited to parking on the facts of that case. The question is legal possession and control — ownership, and the ability to grant further rights — not how much day-to-day practical use is left.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that best supports treating this right as accommodating the dominant tenement, applying Regency Villas.
testPool.scenarioText: A timeshare resort grants owners of each apartment the right to use an adjoining spa and swimming pool complex. The right is expressed to benefit each apartment and its successive owners, and was a key part of why buyers chose to purchase there rather than a comparable resort without such facilities.
tappableSpans: benefit each apartment and its successive owners
why buyers chose to purchase there
testPool.correctSpan: benefit each apartment and its successive owners
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Tying the right to the apartments and their successive owners — rather than to a named individual — is what makes it capable of accommodating the dominant land, exactly as Regency Villas required.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact that ties the right to the land itself, running with successive owners, rather than the commercial attractiveness of the deal to any one buyer. That's the accommodation hook Regency Villas relies on.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is more likely to satisfy the accommodation requirement, applying Regency Villas rather than failing like Hill v Tupper?
testPool.scenarioA: A resort grants the current manager of a nearby unrelated business a personal right to use its gym for free, unconnected to any land the manager owns.
testPool.scenarioB: A resort grants each owner of a specific block of holiday apartments, and their successors in title, the right to use its gym and pool facilities.
testPool.explanation: B ties the right to specific dominant land (the apartments) and their successive owners, exactly the structure Regency Villas upheld. A is Hill v Tupper again — a personal benefit to an individual, disconnected from any land they own.

testPool.prompt: A developer sells off a house with the benefit of a right to use a shared ornamental garden on adjoining land retained by the developer, for the pleasure of residents of that house and their successors. The developer's successor now denies the right is an easement, arguing a garden confers only a personal amenity. Analyse whether the right is capable of being an easement.
factsToOrder: The house is the dominant tenement and the garden is the servient tenement
The right is expressed to benefit the house and its successive owners, not a named individual
The garden and house are in different ownership
The right is to use a garden for pleasure and recreation, closely analogous to Re Ellenborough Park
The developer's successor argues the right is merely a personal amenity

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the right to use the shared garden is capable of being an easement attached to the house.
modelAnswer.rule: Re Ellenborough Park requires a dominant and servient tenement, accommodation of the dominant tenement, different owners, and that the right be capable of forming the subject matter of a grant; a right to use a garden for pleasure and recreation, tied to the dominant land and its successive owners, satisfies all four.
modelAnswer.application: The house and garden are in different ownership, satisfying tenements and separate ownership. Because the right benefits the house and successive owners rather than a named individual, it accommodates the dominant tenement on facts essentially identical to Ellenborough Park itself. The developer's 'merely personal amenity' argument fails for the same reason Hill v Tupper's argument would have succeeded had it been run the other way: the right here runs with the land, not with a person.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The right is capable of being an easement; it satisfies all four Ellenborough Park characteristics on facts closely matching that case.

testPool.prompt: Did Moncrieff v Jamieson concern a parking right or a right of way?
options: A parking right
A right of way

testPool.prompt: Which statement best captures what Regency Villas decided about the accommodation requirement?
options: A right can accommodate the dominant tenement by enhancing its normal enjoyment even where the benefit is recreational rather than strictly utilitarian
Recreational rights can never be easements, since accommodation requires a utilitarian benefit like access or drainage
Regency Villas replaced the accommodation requirement entirely with a pure commercial-value test
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answer assumes accommodation must be utilitarian — exactly the argument the Supreme Court rejected. Regency Villas confirms recreational benefit can accommodate land; it does not abolish the requirement or replace it with a commercial test.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common failure in this lesson's items is stopping the checklist early — confirming a dominant and servient tenement exist and assuming the rest follows. Nearly every trap here is hidden in characteristic 2 (accommodation) or characteristic 4 (capable of forming the subject matter of a grant), not in the first, easiest-to-spot characteristic.
